title: Dropping shell=True in subprocess calls
summary: See rule DPK-SAST-003 fire on a synthetic Python report job that runs a subprocess with shell=True, replace the shell string with an argument list, and verify the finding is gone on rescan.
concept: Passing shell=True to subprocess runs the command string through the system shell. Any attacker-influenced part of that string can add shell metacharacters (;, &&, |, backticks) and turn one intended command into several — command injection. The safe pattern is an argument list with shell=False: the arguments are passed to the program directly and are never re-parsed as shell syntax. This lesson pairs with pack rule DPK-SAST-003, which flags the lexical shape shell=True on one line. The rule cannot prove data flow, so a fully static command with shell=True still fires and the reviewer should note that.
objectives: Explain why a shell command string is an injection surface when any part is dynamic.
Recognise shell=True in review and in scan findings.
Replace the shell string with an argument list and verify by rescan.

practice.instruction: Import the starter file into one of your OWN projects, run a SAST scan, and find rule DPK-SAST-003. Read the finding, confirm which part of the command is dynamic, apply the fix (an argument list with shell=False), upload the fixed file, and run SAST again to verify the finding is no longer observed.
practice.fixInstruction: Pass the program and its arguments as a list with shell=False so the date value is never parsed as shell syntax.

quiz.prompt: Why is an argument list with shell=False safer than a shell command string?
options: Arguments are passed to the program directly and are not re-parsed as shell syntax
An argument list is always faster
quiz.explanation: With shell=False the date value stays one argument; with shell=True the shell would split and interpret metacharacters inside it.

quiz.prompt: What does a DPK-SAST-003 finding prove?
options: A shell=True flag is present and the command deserves review — not that the code is exploitable
The value is a live credential
quiz.explanation: The rule is lexical: it flags the flag itself. Review decides whether any part of the command is attacker-influenced.

quiz.prompt: What is the right check after the fix?
options: Rescan and confirm the rule no longer fires on the fixed file
Delete the rule from the scan
Skip the rescan if the code runs
quiz.explanation: A rescan shows the finding is gone for the reviewed code path. Running the code alone does not show that.
